partner_context.their_ambition: The MBTA runs Greater Boston's public-transport network — subway, bus, commuter rail and the Boston Harbor ferries linking downtown to Charlestown, East Boston, the South Shore and North Shore, ticketed through the MBTA system.
partner_context.their_pressure: Massachusetts law mandates net zero by 2050 and the MBTA has committed to fleet electrification — but the harbor ferries still run on diesel, and demand for the Hingham and inner-harbor lines keeps growing. Growth and the net-zero mandate both demand fleet renewal without disturbing the services people rely on today.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: Navier is the zero-emission foiling upgrade to a network the MBTA already runs — faster harbor and South Shore commutes that relieve the expressway and tunnels while delivering the fleet electrification state law requires.

hero.title: Boston Harbor Ferries (MBTA) × Navier — a zero-emission foiling layer on the water
hero.subtitle: A foiling tier above today's network on Boston Harbor and Massachusetts Bay: faster, near-silent, low-wake lines, a clear decarbonization path, and the services people rely on left running underneath.

Massachusetts law mandates net zero by 2050 and the MBTA has committed to fleet electrification — but the harbor ferries still run on diesel, and demand for the Hingham and inner-harbor lines keeps growing.

differentiation.why_navier: Software-defined and autonomy-ready — the same DNA as the autonomous road programs — built for fleet operation, with a ~100-vessel network proving the model in the Maldives.

proof_points.claim: The authority runs marine transport at public scale.
proof_points.evidence: The MBTA runs year-round and seasonal ferries (routes F1–F7) from Long Wharf and Rowes Wharf to Charlestown, East Boston, Hingham, Hull, Winthrop, Lynn and Quincy, integrated into the MBTA network.

proof_points.claim: There is a published growth and decarbonization mandate.
proof_points.evidence: Massachusetts law mandates net zero by 2050 and the MBTA has committed to fleet electrification — but the harbor ferries still run on diesel, and demand for the Hingham and inner-harbor lines keeps growing.
proof_points.source: Massachusetts Clean Energy and Climate Plan 2050

proof_points.evidence: Hydrofoiling, software-governed vessels — the same DNA arriving in autonomous road mobility — built for fleet operation.

proof_points.claim: The fleet model is real and at scale.
proof_points.evidence: ~100 vessels / $100M / 3-year phasing proving the network model in the Maldives; 10 vessels delivered, 4,000+ flight hours; a demo vessel is on the water now.

objections.concern: Does this compete with the existing public ferry service?
objections.response: No — Navier is a passenger-only foiling layer above the existing service, adding fast frequencies on the busy corridors the conventional boats can't run economically. It complements the electrification already underway.
Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal at existing piers — no new shore power, vertiports or rights-of-way.

objections.concern: Is foiling safe in busy, shared public waterways?
objections.response: Foiling is software-governed — geofenced no-foil and low-wake zones near piers, ferry lanes and moorings, automatic speed and wake limits in shared water, and conventional low-speed handling everywhere it isn't cleared to fly.

close.title: A zero-emission water layer that grows with the city.
close.body: Start on the busiest corridors, scale across the full network, then mature the service — a zero-emission foiling tier that advances the authority's net-zero mandate while the services people rely on keep running underneath.

why_navier_now.step_change: Hydrofoiling lifts the hull clear of the water, so a Navier vessel flies instead of plowing through chop — roughly 10x more efficient than a conventional planing boat, faster (30+ kt cruise), and dramatically smoother and quieter. It's software-defined and autonomy-ready, so the same fleet keeps getting better and cheaper to run over time.
why_navier_now.no_new_infrastructure: Navier rides on infrastructure that already exists — the open water and the piers already in use. No vertiports, no new rights-of-way, no tunnels or tracks. Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal; the long-range hybrid needs no charging infrastructure at all.
why_navier_now.the_moment: Three forces just converged: the technology crossed from prototype to platform (10 vessels delivered, 4,000+ flight hours, 2025 production sold out), decarbonization mandates turned legacy diesel fleets into stranded liabilities, and the hybrid removed the charging excuse. The marine layer is being claimed cluster-by-cluster right now.
